newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Questions raised as U.S. arms flow to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Questions raised as U.S. arms flow to Bosnia.

text.p: As the United States finally starts delivery of a huge arms shipment to Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation, embarrassing news is on the way for Washington about problems with a Balkan arms control deal.

Military sources at the Vienna-based Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) say neither the federation nor the Bosnian Serbs are meeting their commitments so far under the arms limitation agreement.

The OSCE has been charged with overseeing a U.S.-backed arms control deal, signed in June, which committed the two sides in Bosnia, as well as Croatia and Serbia, to make cuts in their military hardware such as tanks and artillery.
Both sides in Bosnia are supposed to have destroyed a certain percentage of their excess equipment by the end of this year and to complete the task by October 1997.

"I think it rather unlikely that either the federation or the Republika Srpska (Bosnian Serb entity) will have complied fully with the first phase by the end of this year," one senior military source told Reuters.
The arms control deal was laid down as part of the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace agreement, signed one year ago.

Washington has enthusiastically backed the arms control measures while insisting that it would still be able to provide weapons and training to the Moslem-Croat federation -- despite some unease among its European allies.

The United States says the tanks, artillery pieces and vehicles which are to be unloaded at the Croatian port of Ploce will improve the quality of the federation's forces without violating arms control provisions on equipment amounts.
The equipment will help make the Moslems and Croats a military match for the Bosnian Serbs, seen as powerful aggressors by Washington in the 43-month conflict.
Norwegian General Vigleik Eide, in charge of monitoring the arms accord, told Reuters the U.S. shipment was not a violation of the agreement in any sense.
Although he thought it would finally be implemented, he admitted there were problems in monitoring the pact and making sure the parties complied.

While Serbia and Croatia were on schedule with promised disarmament, the Bosnian Serbs had tried to use loopholes in the treaty to win exemptions and Eide said "they seem to have been incomplete" in reporting how much hardware they have.

Problems with making the Moslem-Croat federation work in a military and political sense had caused trouble in providing data about equipment to be destroyed and caused disagreements about how to share out the reductions.
The Moslems and Croats fought each other at one stage during the war and there is still much mutual mistrust.
"They have not really started their first-phase reductions and time is pressing," Eide said.

In their case, more than 1,000 artillery pieces have to be destroyed since the federation does not have many tanks or armoured vehicles. Military sources say the Bosnian Serbs need to destroy nearly 2,000 big guns, tanks and armoured vehicles.
